title: Barcodes and QR Codes
summary: How tiny patterns of black lines and squares let machines read prices and information in an instant, and who invented them.
poll: Shopping would be slower and less accurate without barcodes and QR codes.

versions.title: The Lines That Tell a Story
versions.text:
Look at a box in a shop. You will see black lines. This is a barcode.

A barcode is a pattern of lines. Each line is thick or thin.

A cashier uses a scanner to read it. The scanner shines light on the code. The light bounces back.

The lines stand for a number. The number tells the price of the thing. This is called the product.

Long ago, a cashier had to type each price by hand. That took time. It could be wrong too.

Some codes are not lines. They are small black squares. We call this a QR code.

A phone can scan a QR code. Then it can open a web page!

Codes like this help shops work fast.

Look at a box in a store. You will see a pattern of black lines printed on it. This pattern is called a barcode.

A barcode is made of thick and thin lines. Each product in the store has its own barcode, almost like a short name written in lines.

A cashier uses a machine called a scanner to read it. The scanner shines a beam of light onto the code. The light bounces back, and a small computer reads it.

The lines stand for a number. That number tells the price of the item. The computer looks up the correct price very fast.

Long ago, a cashier had to type every price by hand. That took a lot of time, and people sometimes made mistakes.

Not every code is made of lines. Some codes are small black and white squares. We call this a QR code.

A smartphone's camera can scan a QR code in less than a second. Then it can open a web page or show a menu.

Barcodes and QR codes now help stores, hospitals, and airports work fast and correctly.

versions.title: Barcodes and QR Codes
versions.text:
Almost every product in a store has a pattern of black lines. This is called a barcode. It stores information: a number that tells a computer the price and the name of the item.

A cashier reads a barcode with a scanner. The scanner shines a laser onto the lines. The light bounces back, and a computer turns it into a number. That number is sent to the store's database for an accurate price. This all happens in less than a second.

Before barcodes, workers had to type each price by hand. This was slow. It was not very accurate, since a tired worker could press the wrong key after a long day.

The barcode idea came from two inventors, Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver, in 1952. Woodland got the idea while drawing lines in beach sand with his fingers. He wanted a universal code that any store could use. In 1974, a pack of chewing gum became the first product ever scanned at a real store.

A QR code can hold more information than a barcode. It can even hold a whole web address. A phone camera can scan it fast to open a page or show a menu.

Barcodes and QR codes are used almost everywhere now. Stores, hospitals, and busy warehouses all use them to track items every single day.

This all happens in less than a second.

The barcode idea came from two American inventors, Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver, who worked on it in 1952. Woodland is said to have gotten the idea while drawing lines in beach sand with his fingers, wondering how to build a universal code. In 1974, a pack of chewing gum became the very first product ever scanned at a real supermarket.

A QR code can hold far more information than a barcode. It can even hold a whole web address. A smartphone camera can scan it in an instant to open a page or confirm a payment.

Barcodes and QR codes are used almost everywhere now. Stores, hospitals, and busy warehouses must accurately track thousands of boxes every single day.

versions.title: Barcodes and QR Codes
versions.text:
Almost every product sold in a retail store carries a pattern of black lines and white spaces known as a barcode. This pattern actually encodes important information: a number that identifies the exact item, its manufacturer, and often its size or color.

A cashier reads a barcode with a scanner, a device that sweeps a laser or a bright beam of light across the lines. The reflected light lets a connected computer decode the pattern into a number almost instantly. That number is sent to the retailer's database, which finds an accurate price and description within a tiny fraction of a second, saving the cashier and the customer valuable time.

Before barcodes existed, workers had to type every price by hand on a cash register. This method was slow, and it was not especially accurate, since a tired worker could easily press the wrong key after a long shift.

The barcode idea came from two American inventors, Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver, who developed it in 1952 and were granted a patent for their invention the next year. Woodland is said to have first imagined the idea while drawing lines in beach sand, wondering how to design a universal code that any retailer around the world could use. It took more than twenty years for the technology to catch on: in 1974, a pack of chewing gum became the first product ever scanned at a real supermarket checkout in Ohio.

A newer kind of code, the QR code, was invented in Japan and can encode far more information than a barcode, including a whole web address. Three large squares printed in its corners help a scanner's camera figure out the code's orientation, no matter which way it is held or turned.

Barcodes and QR codes are now used almost everywhere, from stores and hospitals to enormous warehouses that must accurately track thousands of boxes every single day.

versions.title: Barcodes and QR Codes
versions.text:
Almost every product sold in a retail establishment carries a seemingly unassuming pattern of black lines and white spaces known, somewhat prosaically, as a barcode. This pattern actually encodes genuinely valuable information: a numeric identifier that specifies the exact item, its manufacturer, and frequently its size or color.

A cashier reads a barcode with a scanner, a device that sweeps a laser or a bright beam of light systematically across the lines. The reflected light enables a connected computer to decode the pattern into a number almost instantaneously. That number is subsequently transmitted to the retailer's database, which retrieves an accurate price and description within a tiny fraction of a second, sparing the cashier and the customer considerable time while substantially reducing the chance of a costly human error.

Before barcodes existed, employees were obliged to type every single price by hand on a cash register. This method was inherently slow, and it was not especially accurate, since even a conscientious worker could easily strike the wrong key after a long, tiring shift on a particularly busy day.

The concept of the barcode originated with two American inventors, Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver, who developed the idea in 1952 and were granted a patent for their invention the following year, long before the necessary scanning technology had even been adequately perfected for commercial use. Woodland is said to have first envisioned the idea while absentmindedly drawing lines in beach sand, wondering how he might design a genuinely universal code that any retailer around the world could eventually adopt regardless of language or currency. It took more than two decades for the technology to achieve widespread commercial adoption: in 1974, a pack of chewing gum became the first product ever scanned at a genuine supermarket checkout in Ohio.

A considerably newer kind of code, the QR code, was invented in Japan during the 1990s by an engineer named Masahiro Hara, who designed it to help factories track engine parts far more efficiently than existing barcodes permitted. A QR code can encode considerably more information than a traditional barcode, including an entire web address. Three large squares printed in its corners help a scanner's camera determine the code's orientation instantly, regardless of which way the code happens to be held or rotated, a feature that makes it remarkably convenient to scan while on the move.

Barcodes and QR codes are now employed in countless settings, from stores, hospitals, and libraries to airports, where they appear on boarding passes, and enormous warehouses that must accurately track thousands upon thousands of boxes every single day. Even so, a damaged, faded, or poorly printed barcode can occasionally fail to scan correctly, forcing a retailer's staff back to the slower, markedly less reliable method of entering a number by hand, a reminder that even remarkably reliable technology still benefits from a dependable human backup.

wrong.B: The article does not argue against QR codes.
wrong.D: Chewing gum is mentioned only once, as an example.

MID.prompt: Explain how a barcode gets scanned and turned into a price, using at least three steps from the article in order.
checklist: I explained the steps in the correct order.
I used at least three details from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
MID.modelAnswer: First, a cashier uses a scanner that shines a laser across the barcode's lines. Then a connected computer translates the reflected light into a number almost instantly. Finally, that number is sent to the store's database, which looks up the accurate price and name of the product.

keyWords.definition: an official document that gives a person the only right to make or sell their invention
keyWords.example: The young engineer applied for a patent on her new solar charger.

keyWords.definition: the direction something is facing or turned
keyWords.example: The arrow on the map showed the orientation of north.

keyWords.definition: a business that sells goods directly to shoppers
keyWords.example: The retailer added extra cashiers before the holiday rush.

keyWords.definition: to put information into a special form, such as a code
keyWords.example: Programmers encode messages so computers can store them.

keyWords.definition: a person who creates something new for the first time
keyWords.example: The young inventor built a machine that waters plants automatically.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of this article?
options: Barcodes and QR codes encode information, and engineers invented both to speed up and improve accuracy in buying and tracking goods over time.
QR codes replaced most traditional barcodes in stores around the world because they look more modern and are cheaper to print on paper and plastic bags.
Factories in Japan were the first to use QR codes, and they still use them more than others.
Supermarkets around the world no longer need cash registers today.
questions.why: The article traces how both codes were invented and how they encode information to make buying and tracking goods faster and more accurate.

wrong.B: QR codes were invented decades after 1952, and barcodes are still used.
wrong.C: The article shows QR codes used in stores, hospitals, and airports, not only factories.
wrong.D: Cash registers are still used with scanners in the article.

questions.stem: Who invented the idea for the barcode, and in what year?
options: Engineers at Denso Wave in Japan, in 1952
Masahiro Hara, working in Japan, in the 1990s
Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver, in 1952
A busy supermarket cashier at work, in 1974
questions.why: The article states that Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver developed the barcode idea in 1952.

wrong.A: Denso Wave is connected to the QR code, not the barcode.
wrong.B: Masahiro Hara invented the QR code decades later.
wrong.D: A cashier scanned the first product in 1974 but did not invent the idea.

questions.stem: Why did Masahiro Hara originally develop the QR code?
options: To replace cash registers inside every single store
To let people pay for packs of chewing gum more easily
To help factories track car or engine parts more efficiently
To design a brand new kind of scanner just for libraries
questions.why: Hara made the QR code to help factories keep track of car parts more easily.

wrong.A: Cash registers are not mentioned as his goal.
wrong.B: Chewing gum relates to the first barcode scan, not the QR code's invention.
wrong.D: Libraries are mentioned only as a place where codes are later used.

questions.stem: In the article, what does orientation mean?
options: The price of a product
A business that sells goods to shoppers in the city
A kind of database used by a retailer
The direction something is facing or turned
questions.why: The article explains that the corner squares help a camera determine the code's orientation, meaning which way it is turned.

wrong.A: Price is a separate idea in the article.
wrong.B: That describes a retailer, a different term.
wrong.C: A database stores information; it is not the meaning of orientation.

questions.stem: Why do the three squares in a QR code's corners matter?
options: They store the exact product's price, its full name, and its maker's details
They stop the printed code from ever being copied or faked by anyone
They help a scanner's camera figure out the code's orientation no matter how it is turned
They simply make the small printed code look more decorative to shoppers nearby in the store
questions.why: The article explains that the corner squares let a camera determine the code's orientation instantly, however it is held or rotated.

wrong.A: Price is encoded elsewhere in the code, not stored by the corner squares.
wrong.B: Copy protection is not mentioned.
wrong.D: The squares serve a functional purpose, not a decorative one.

questions.stem: Why did it take more than two decades after 1952 for barcodes to be used in a real store?
options: No one wanted to buy chewing gum before the year 1974
Supermarkets did not exist anywhere in the world before the year 1974
Barcodes were against the law in stores until 1974
The necessary scanning technology had not yet been fully developed
questions.why: The article notes that the patent came long before the scanning technology needed to use barcodes commercially was ready.

wrong.A: Demand for gum is not the reason given.
wrong.B: Supermarkets already existed before 1974.
wrong.C: No law against barcodes is mentioned.

questions.stem: How does a QR code generally differ from a traditional barcode, according to the article?
options: A QR code can encode far more information, including entire web addresses
A QR code cannot possibly be read by any kind of scanner, ever
A barcode can be used a single time
A QR code must be black and white, while a barcode can be in color or in gray
questions.why: In the article, a QR code can encode considerably more information than a traditional barcode, including whole web addresses.

wrong.B: Smartphone cameras are described scanning QR codes.
wrong.C: Barcodes are read repeatedly at checkouts, not used only once.
wrong.D: Color is not discussed as a difference between the two codes.

questions.stem: How does the article mainly develop its explanation of these codes?
options: By arguing firmly and repeatedly that stores should stop using scanners
By tracing each code's invention, how it works, and where it is used today
By simply comparing the price of gum in 1974 with today's current prices
By telling a long and detailed fictional story about one lost barcode
questions.why: The article moves through how barcodes work, their invention, the QR code's invention, and present-day uses.

wrong.A: The article does not argue against scanners.
wrong.C: Prices are not compared over time.
wrong.D: No fictional story appears in the article.

HIGH.prompt: The article describes two inventions: the barcode and the QR code. Compare why each one was first created, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained why each code was first created.
I used evidence from the article for each code.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver developed the barcode in 1952, hoping to create a universal code that any retailer could use to look up prices accurately instead of typing them by hand. Decades later, Masahiro Hara invented the QR code in Japan during the 1990s so that factories could track car or engine parts more efficiently, and because a QR code can encode far more information than a barcode, including entire web addresses, it eventually found many more uses beyond factories.

LOW.stem: What does the number in a barcode tell the cashier?
options: How old the box is
Where the shop is
The price of the thing
How big the scanner is
LOW.why: The text says the lines stand for a number that tells the price of the product.

wrong.A: The text does not say the number shows the age of the box.
wrong.B: The number is about the product, not the shop.
wrong.D: The number has nothing to do with the scanner size.

LOW.stem: What must happen so the scanner can read the lines?
options: The light bounces back
The cashier types a price
The box is put in water
The lines turn into squares
LOW.why: The text says the scanner shines light and the light bounces back, so the code can be read.

wrong.B: Typing prices is the old way, before barcodes.
wrong.C: The text never says the box goes in water.
wrong.D: Squares are a different kind of code.

LOW.stem: In the article, what is a product?
options: A kind of scanner
A shop worker
A type of phone
A thing for sale
LOW.why: In the text, each product is a thing for sale in a store.

wrong.A: The scanner reads the code, but it is not the product.
wrong.B: The cashier is the shop worker.
wrong.C: A phone scans a QR code but is not called the product.

LOW.stem: How does a QR code look different from a barcode?
options: It has long red lines
It has small black squares
It has only one thick line
It has no black color
LOW.why: In the text, a barcode is made of lines and a QR code is made of small black squares.

wrong.A: The text does not mention red lines.
wrong.C: A barcode has many thick and thin lines.
wrong.D: The QR code is black.

MID.stem: Who first got the barcode idea while drawing in beach sand?
options: Bernard Silver
Norman Woodland
A tired cashier
A store owner
MID.why: In the text, Woodland got the idea while drawing lines in beach sand with his fingers.

wrong.A: Silver worked with Woodland, but Woodland drew in the sand.
wrong.C: The cashier is only named as the person who typed prices.
wrong.D: The text does not mention a store owner.

MID.stem: Why does the scanner send the number to the store's database?
options: To clean the laser light
To tell the cashier a story
To keep the line pattern safe
To find an accurate price
MID.why: The text says the number is sent to the database for an accurate price.

wrong.A: The text does not say the database cleans the laser.
wrong.B: The database gives a price, not a story.
wrong.C: The database is used to find the price, not to protect the lines.

MID.stem: In the article, what does accurate mean?
options: Right, with no errors
Very fast and loud
Easy to carry back home
Cheap and brand new
MID.why: The text says typing was not accurate because a tired worker could press the wrong key.

wrong.B: Speed is a different idea from being accurate.
wrong.C: Carrying is not mentioned with accurate.
wrong.D: The word has nothing to do with cost.

MID.stem: Why can a phone use a QR code to show a menu?
options: The code is bigger than a barcode
The scanner shines a bright laser
The code can hold a web address
The phone has a tiny database
MID.why: A QR code can hold a web address, so a phone camera can scan it and open a page such as a menu.

wrong.A: The text does not say a QR code is bigger.
wrong.B: A laser is used by a barcode scanner, not by a phone camera.
wrong.D: A database is used by a store, not a phone, in this text.

HIGH.stem: Besides the exact item, what else does a barcode number identify?
options: The name of the cashier
The color of the store
The date it was sold
The product's manufacturer
HIGH.why: The barcode number tells the exact item, who made it, and often its size or color.

wrong.A: The cashier is not named in the barcode.
wrong.B: The text says the item may have a color, not the store.
wrong.C: The sale date is not mentioned.

HIGH.stem: In the article, what does the word decode mean?
options: To read a pattern as a number
To print black lines on a box
To type a price in by hand
To pay for an item at a till
HIGH.why: In the text, the computer decodes the pattern into a number almost instantly.

wrong.B: Printing is how the pattern is made, not decoded.
wrong.C: Typing by hand is the old method.
wrong.D: Paying is done after the price is found.

HIGH.stem: What does "is said to have" suggest about the story of the sand?
options: It was filmed by a cashier
It happened at a supermarket
It is a list of facts and dates
It may not be fully proven
HIGH.why: The phrase "is said to have" shows the story is told by people and may not be proven.

wrong.A: The text does not mention any film.
wrong.B: The sand story was at a beach, not a supermarket.
wrong.C: The phrase is not used for exact dates.

HIGH.stem: What happened in 1953, the year after the barcode idea was developed?
options: A pack of gum was scanned in a shop
The inventors got a patent
The QR code was invented in Japan
Barcodes were used in Ohio first
HIGH.why: In the text, the inventors developed it in 1952 and were granted a patent the next year.

wrong.A: The gum was scanned in 1974.
wrong.C: The text does not give a date for the QR code.
wrong.D: Barcodes were used in Ohio only in 1974.
